# The Workstation theme reveal paints black outside the circle

## Context

The operator, comparing the two callers of the engine's theme reveal: in the Portal the circle expands and the **old theme** is visible outside it. In `apps/workstation` — shipped by me in #18125 / PR #18127 — everything outside the circle is **pitch black**.

**Live latest-open sweep:** checked the latest 12 open issues at 2026-09-02T18:40Z; no equivalent found. `#17739` (closed) was the reveal's *geometry*, not its layer compositing. **Own-assignment sweep:** nothing on this surface. **Grep:** no ticket mentions the view-transition pseudo-elements.

## The Problem

`document.startViewTransition()` snapshots the document into two pseudo-elements and, **by UA default, cross-fades them**: `::view-transition-old(root)` fades out and `::view-transition-new(root)` fades in, each over ~250ms, with `mix-blend-mode: plus-lighter` on the image pair.

`DomUtils.createRevealAnimation()` animates **only the new layer** — `clip-path: circle(0% → radius)` over 500ms (`DomUtils.mjs:108`, `pseudoElement: '::view-transition-new(root)'`). It never touches the old layer.

So the old snapshot is gone at ~250ms while the reveal is still growing until 500ms. For the second half of the animation there is nothing underneath the circle, and the viewer sees the bare backdrop — black. The effect is loudest in a dense app, where losing the old snapshot means losing an entire screen of panes, grids and text rather than a mostly-empty page.

**The Portal does not have this problem because it cancels the UA default itself**, in its own stylesheet:

```scss
// resources/scss/src/apps/portal/Viewport.scss:10
::view-transition-old(root),
::view-transition-new(root) {
    animation     : none;
    mix-blend-mode: normal;
}
```

`animation: none` holds both layers at full opacity for the whole transition, so the old one survives until the reveal finishes. `mix-blend-mode: normal` overrides `plus-lighter`, which otherwise blows out overlapping layers.

**The census is the whole defect:**

| app | calls `startViewTransition` | ships the pseudo-element rule |
|---|---|---|
| `apps/portal` | 1 | **1** |
| `apps/workstation` | 1 | **0** |

Verified at runtime on the served Workstation: enumerating `document.styleSheets` for any rule matching `view-transition-(old\|new)\(root\)` returns **none**, while the Portal's is present.

## The Architectural Reality

The reveal is an **engine** capability whose contract is split across two realms, and only one half is in the engine:

- `Neo.main.DomAccess#startViewTransition()` + `DomUtils.createRevealAnimation()` own the *animation*.
- The UA-default cancellation that makes the animation *visible* is CSS, and today it lives in one consumer's app stylesheet.

Nothing tells the second consumer that half the contract exists. I reused the primitive, matched the Portal's call byte-for-byte, verified the payload and keyframes at the runtime boundary, and still shipped a black screen — because the missing piece is not on the call path at all.

## The Fix

Ship the rule in `resources/scss/src/apps/workstation/Workspace.scss`, with a comment naming what it cancels and why the consumer currently has to.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC-1** — switching the Workstation theme shows the **previous theme** outside the growing circle, in both directions, on the served app. No black frame at any point in the animation.
- [ ] **AC-2** — a rule matching `::view-transition-old(root)` is present in the Workstation's loaded stylesheets, asserted by enumerating `document.styleSheets` rather than by reading the SCSS.
- [ ] **AC-3** — the Portal is untouched and still correct.
- [ ] **AC-4 (real browser)** — read by eye. `startViewTransition` is unsupported headless (`pr-13430`), so the compositing itself cannot be witnessed by any headless arm; AC-2 is the mechanical proxy and this is the visual confirmation.

## Out of Scope

- **Moving the rule into the engine**, which is the correct long-term answer and is filed separately — see Related. Tonight's change is the consumer-side repair the rehearsal needs; the engine change alters compositing for every consumer and is not a thing to land hours before a demo.
- The reveal's geometry, duration and easing — all correct and unchanged.

## Avoided Traps

- **Copying the Portal's rule without naming what it does.** Two bare declarations with no comment is how this became invisible in the first place; the next reader must be able to see that it cancels a UA default rather than adding decoration.
- **Reaching for the engine fix tonight.** It is right, and it is a compositing change for every consumer with a rehearsal in the morning.

## Related

- #18125 / PR #18127 — the change that introduced the second caller. This is its regression and mine.
- #17739 / PR #17743 — the reveal's geometry contract.

**Successor filed:** the engine-side generalisation this ticket's Out of Scope pointed at is **#18138** — *"The reveal's UA-default cancellation lives in consumer stylesheets, not the engine"*. It was filed at 19:18Z, three minutes after this body was written, so the Out of Scope section names it without a number.

#18138 carries the census that makes the case (`portal calls=1 rule=1`, `workstation calls=1 rule=0`), an explicit AC to **retire both consumer rules in the same change** so the workaround does not gain a third copy, and one deliberately unverified premise — that a WAAPI animation outranks the UA's CSS animation on the same pseudo-element — stated as a candidate with a measure-it AC rather than a prescription. It is parked with a rationale rather than silently: it alters compositing for every consumer, and the rehearsal is tomorrow morning.

Also added on this ticket's PR (#18137) after @neo-opus-grace's review: the rule's comment now records that it **must stay at file top level**. These are document pseudo-elements — nesting them under `.workstation-workspace` for tidiness would not scope them, it would make them never match, silently, with a black reveal as the only symptom and nothing pointing back at the refactor. This file's own comment three lines below establishes the vessel-versus-workspace reasoning that would tempt exactly that change, which is what makes the trap worth naming in place.
